progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c08a (oxidation removes two H and forms C=O, the carbonyl group; primary to aldehyde to acid, secondary to ketone, tertiary no reaction; distil for the aldehyde; acidified dichromate orange to green; "-al" and "-one" read as endings); chem-m7-c05 (alcohol naming, hydrogen bonding between O–H groups, boiling points, solubility, "Same size? Hydrogen bonding wins."); chem-m7-c03 (dispersion forces, the water lattice, "like dissolves like"); chem-m7-c01 and g01 (naming rules, locants, branches); chem-m7-c02 (isomers). Year 11: electronegativity, polar bonds, lone pairs, dipole–dipole forces, reduction as gain of electrons. Not assumed: aldehyde and ketone naming rules, functional group isomer (c02 named structural isomers; this video adds the functional group kind with a plain meaning), Tollens', Fehling's, Benedict's, precipitate (Year 11 term, given a plain meaning).
progression.startsWith: Locate the carbonyl and name aldehydes and ketones. The video opens: In the alcohol reactions video, oxidising propan-two-ol gave a ketone, propanone. Oxidise propan-one-ol and distil, as we did with ethanol, and you get an aldehyde, propanal. Both have the formula C three H six O.
progression.stopsAfter: identifying an aldehyde or ketone from the carbonyl's position; naming both up to C8 with methyl or ethyl branches; recognising functional group isomers; explaining their boiling points and solubility from their forces; explaining why an aldehyde gives a positive Tollens', Fehling's or dichromate test and a ketone does not; using a test on an oxidation product to identify the alcohol's class. No carboxylic acid properties, no practical procedure.
progression.nextLesson: oxidising alcohols and testing the products in the lab (route chem-m7-p04, "Investigate alcohol oxidation products").

teaching.task: Oxidise propan-1-ol and distil, and you get propanal; oxidise propan-2-ol, and you get propanone. Both are C₃H₆O, and both are colourless liquids, yet only one turns a test tube into a silver mirror. How do we name aldehydes and ketones, how does the carbonyl's position change their properties, and how can a test tell them apart?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) propanal and propanone share a formula, yet one gives a silver mirror (1); (2) both have a polar carbonyl; the aldehyde's is at the end, so its carbonyl carbon carries an H; the ketone's is inside, with a carbon each side (2); (3) aldehyde names: "-al", the carbonyl carbon is C1, so no number (3); (4) ketone names: "-one", a number from C5, from the end nearer the C=O (4); (5) same formula, different group: functional group isomers, easy to miss (5); (6) the polar C=O gives dipole–dipole forces, but no O–H means no hydrogen bonding between their molecules, so their boiling points sit between alkane and alcohol (6); (7) the aldehyde H is on carbon, so it can't hydrogen bond; water can hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen, so small ones dissolve (7); (8) the aldehyde's carbonyl H lets mild oxidants oxidise it, and the reduced reagent changes visibly; a ketone has none (8); (9) Tollens': silver ions reduced to a silver mirror (9); (10) Fehling's: blue copper(II) reduced to a brick-red copper(I) oxide precipitate (10); (11) dichromate too; all three ask one question (11); (12) testing the distilled product identifies the alcohol's class; dichromate alone can't (12); memory aid (13); two attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: oxidising propan-1-ol and distilling gives propanal while propan-2-ol gives propanone, both C3H6O, yet only one makes a silver mirror, so the video asks how to name aldehydes and ketones, how the carbonyl's position shapes their forces, and how a test tells them apart. Both have a polar C=O; an aldehyde's carbonyl is at the end of the chain, so its carbon carries a hydrogen, while a ketone's sits inside with a carbon on each side. Aldehydes take al with no number because the carbonyl carbon is carbon one; ketones take one, with a number from five carbons, counted from the end nearer the C=O; the pair are functional group isomers. The polar C=O gives dipole-dipole forces but no hydrogen bonds between the molecules, so boiling points sit between the alkane and the alcohol, while water can hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen, so small ones dissolve. The aldehyde's one hydrogen lets mild oxidants oxidise it: Tollens' reagent leaves a silver mirror, Fehling's or Benedict's solution turns from blue to a brick-red precipitate, and acidified dichromate turns green, while a ketone leaves each unchanged. Testing the distilled product of an oxidation identifies the alcohol's class. The memory aid is aldehyde at the end, ketone in the middle, and every test asks whether there is an H on the carbonyl carbon. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In the alcohol reactions video, oxidising propan-two-ol gave a ketone, propanone. Oxidise propan-one-ol and distil, as we did with ethanol, and you get an aldehyde, propanal. Both have the formula C three H six O. Both are colourless liquids. Yet warm each one with this reagent, and one coats the tube in a silver mirror, while the other does nothing. What's the difference, and how do we name and test these compounds?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A compound has the condensed structural formula CH₃CH₂COCH(CH₃)CH₃. State whether it is an aldehyde or a ketone, giving a reason, and give its IUPAC name." A skeletal formula is shown beside it in plain ink (no colours, no locants). New molecule (scenes use straight-chain pentanones and 2-methylpropanal); tests the carbonyl's position and branch numbering. Crossed mistake: "4-methylpentan-3-one" (numbered from the wrong end; the c01 and c05 feedback pattern). (A2) "Compounds A and B both have the molecular formula C₄H₈O, and both contain a C=O group. When each is warmed with Tollens' reagent, A forms a silver mirror and B shows no change. A has an unbranched chain. Identify A and B by IUPAC name, and explain the difference in their results." New pair (scenes use propanal and propanone); tests the one-hydrogen reason. Crossed mistake: "Both have a C=O group, so both should form a mirror." (the site's Common Error, Fehling's version).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the nomenclature of organic chemicals, up to C8, using IUPAC conventions, including simple methyl and ethyl branched chains, including: (ACSCH127); alkanes; alkenes; alkynes; alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary); aldehydes and ketones; carboxylic acids; amines and amides; halogenated organic compounds" This video covers aldehydes and ketones only (hydrocarbons chem-m7-c01 and g01; haloalkanes chem-m7-c04a; alcohols chem-m7-c05). "investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including:; primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols; aldehydes and ketones (ACSCH127); amines and amides; carboxylic acids" This video covers aldehydes and ketones (alcohols chem-m7-c05; carboxylic acids chem-m7-c09; amines and amides chem-m7-c11). "investigate the products of the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols" This video shows how the products are told apart; chem-m7-c08a predicted them, and chem-m7-p04 carries out the investigation. this video starts by locating the carbonyl group in an aldehyde and a ketone and naming both families, and stops at explaining how tests distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone and using them to identify the product of an alcohol oxidation. It teaches: the carbonyl group (recalled from c08a) is polar because oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly; in an aldehyde the C=O is at the end of the chain and the carbonyl carbon carries an H (–CHO); in a ketone the C=O is inside the chain, with a carbon on each side and no H on the carbonyl carbon; naming aldehydes (longest chain including the carbonyl carbon, drop the final "e", add "al"; the carbonyl carbon is C1, so no locant; branches numbered from it: 2-methylpropanal); naming ketones ("one"; propanone and butanone need no locant; from C5 a locant from the end nearer the C=O: pentan-2-one, pentan-3-one; branches as in c01); aldehydes and ketones with the same number of carbons (three or more) are functional group isomers (propanal and propanone, C₃H₆O); intermolecular forces: dipole–dipole from the C=O plus dispersion, and no hydrogen bonding between their own molecules (no O–H), so for similar sizes their boiling points sit between an alkane and an alcohol; the aldehyde H is on carbon, not oxygen, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond; water can hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen's lone pairs, so small aldehydes and ketones dissolve in water, less as the chain grows; tests: the aldehyde's carbonyl H lets it be oxidised by mild oxidising agents while the reagent is reduced; Tollens' reagent (silver ions in ammonia solution, warmed) gives a silver mirror with an aldehyde and no change with a ketone; Fehling's or Benedict's solution (blue, copper(II)) gives a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide with an aldehyde and stays blue with a ketone; acidified dichromate turns green with an aldehyde and stays orange with a ketone; using a test on the distilled product of an alcohol oxidation to identify a primary or secondary alcohol, and why dichromate alone cannot (primary and secondary alcohols turn it green too); Tollens' hazard: made fresh, used at once and disposed of promptly, because on standing it can form an explosive solid. Not here: alcohol reactions and conditions (chem-m7-c08a, recalled); carboxylic acids, their dimers, boiling points and acidity (chem-m7-c09); the practical procedure, reagent preparation and risk table (chem-m7-p04, with `C7-IQ2-05`); half-equations for the tests (author note d); aromatic aldehydes and ketones (vanillin, raspberry ketone; author note g); reduction of carbonyl compounds; aldehyde and ketone uses beyond one hook line; cyclic ketones; the site's olfactory-receptor discussion.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c08a: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey (the aldehyde's carbonyl H grey-white and slightly larger); main chain pale blue; branches amber; oxygen brick red, the C=O ringed red as the functional group; δ− and δ+ small in navy; lone pairs as two small red dot pairs on O; dipole–dipole attractions dotted teal; hydrogen bonds dotted violet; dispersion forces dotted pale blue. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Aldehyde or ketone?", "Name it", "Forces", "Test it"); centre the structure board, one molecule or one pair at a time; the boiling point strip at the right only in scene 6; plates small or medium at the left or right only in scenes 1, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 17. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous case leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 23 Oct): `m8-dichromate-orange-v1.png` and `m8-dichromate-green-v1.png` (aligned pair, as in c08a; scene 11, small; same pre-build alpha check as c08a). No other existing plate fits: the `c5-copper-tube-*` pair shows a copper(II) equilibrium colour shift, not a precipitate; `m7-bromine-water-pair-v1.png` is a different test. Four new plates (two aligned pairs; Assets). All plates small or medium, scale uniformly only, never stretched. No human figures.
